title: BRST quantization for the restoration of broken symmetries: a pedagogical example
abstract: We present a pedagogical showcase of BRST quantization for restoring symmetries in nuclear many-body systems as a reformulation and potential alternative to conventional projection methods. The formalism is illustrated using translational invariance for a simple system of two interacting masses in one dimension, but with an eye toward generalizing to more particles, higher dimensions, and other symmetries. We explain the considerations underlying particular choices within the BRST construction, and develop both Hamiltonian and path integral formulations to provide guidance for the variety of many-body and effective field theory contexts where gauge fixing for symmetry restoration might be useful. For the demonstration system we show how to diagonalize within the extended BRST phase space, how variation after projection is recovered for product reference states, how the corresponding gauge-fixed functional integral is constructed, and how collective zero modes are isolated and controlled. Throughout, we keep in mind extensions of BRST symmetry to various approximation schemes as a guide for consistent symmetry restoration.
summary: This paper introduces BRST quantization as a rigorous, systematic method to restore broken symmetries in quantum many-body systems, using a simple two-body model for illustration. It shows that by treating the symmetry as a local gauge symmetry, the formalism correctly cancels spurious degrees of freedom in both Hamiltonian and path integral treatments. This offers a powerful alternative to traditional projection techniques for effective field theories.
main_problem: The paper addresses the theoretical challenge of restoring symmetries in many-body quantum systems when using approximate reference state methods that inherently break these symmetries.
main_result: It demonstrates that BRST quantization provides a systematic and consistent alternative to conventional projection methods for handling symmetry restoration, particularly by converting global symmetries into local gauge symmetries.
method: The core method involves promoting global symmetries to local gauge symmetries, applying the BRST formalism (using ghost variables), and developing both Hamiltonian and path integral formulations to ensure gauge invariance in observables.
model_or_system: The analysis uses a pedagogical two-body system of interacting masses in one dimension, which serves as a model to illustrate the general mechanism applicable to complex many-body systems and effective field theories.
key_observables: Gauge invariant observables, the intrinsic energy spectrum (viewed from the collective rest frame), and the cancellation of spurious dynamics related to the center of mass.
important_parameters: The coupling constant of the potential V, the variational parameter alpha, and the limit $\mu 	o 0$ in the path integral formulation.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the BRST mechanism correctly handles the cancellation of spurious degrees of freedom, and the path integral results are strictly valid only in the limit where the gauge-fixing width parameter $\mu$ vanishes.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the redundancy of gauge orbits in phase space, the transition from global to local symmetry via collective coordinates, and the comparison of energy minimization results using various variational ansätze.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the symmetry restoration problem to reformulating the system using collective coordinates, applying the BRST formalism to derive both Hamiltonian and path integral treatments, and finally comparing the consistency of gauge fixing methods.
why_interesting: The systematic handling of gauge symmetries via BRST quantization is a powerful, general technique applicable to any physical system where approximate methods break continuous symmetries, making it relevant for advanced many-body theory.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: There are multiple physically equivalent trajectories (gauge orbits) in the phase space of a gauge theory. A gauge fixing condition (red line) picks just one point along each set of gauge orbits, defining a “gauge slice”. Figure adapted from [14].

FIG. 2: a) The original system of particles has a global translational symmetry: the system can be uniformly translated to any location on the x axis and have the same intrinsic dynamics. (b) The system can now be moved arbitrarily at each moment in time, with an adjustment in R keeping it fixed as if it is at the same point on the line.

FIG. 3: (a) The coordinate portion of the extended phase space for the two-body system, with the plane defined by the collective coordinate R and the CoM of the original DoFs X = (x1 + x2)/2 highlighted. Physically equivalent configurations of the system generated by the constraint Eq. (7) (also known as gauge orbits) lie on such a plane. (b) The CoM and collective coordinate plane with several options for gauge-fixing illustrated (c.f. the red line in Fig. 1). The choice X = 0 corresponds to the gauge-fixing choice used to exactly diagonalize the Hamiltonian in Sec. IV. The choice R = 0 reduces us back to the original problem.

FIG. 4: Energy as a function of variational parameter α for a Gaussian potential well with (a) a Lorentzian product ansatz and (b) a super-Gaussian product ansatz. Results for VAP, Hint, and plain H are compared to the exact result and PAV evaluated with α∗ H and α∗ Hint.

FIG. 5: Energy as a function of variational parameter α for a Woods-Saxon potential well with (a) a Lorentzian product ansatz and (b) a super-Gaussian product ansatz. Results for VAP, Hint, and plain H are compared to the exact result and PAV evaluated with H and Hint.
